1.e4 e5 2.f4 exf4 3.Nf3 Nc6.name: King's Gambit Accepted: MacLeod Defence
1.e4 e5 2.f4 exf4 3.Nf3 Nc6.background: Named after Nicholas MacLeod. Joe Gallagher writes that it has never really caught on.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 exf4 3.Nf3 Nc6 4.Nc3.strategy: Develops the second knight and guards e4 instead of hurrying to win the f4 pawn back. The knight on c6 does nothing about Black's problem of holding that pawn, so White can build up the attack while Black's king's side stays unprepared.
1.e4 e5 2.f4 exf4 3.Nf3 Nc6 4.Nc3.name: Vienna Gambit, with Max Lange Defence: Knight Variation

1.e4 e5 2.f4 exf4 3.Nf3 Nc6 4.Bc4.strategy: Aims the bishop at f7 straight away, where only the king defends. Black's knight on c6 does not help to keep the f4 pawn, so White can choose between striking in the centre and attacking the kingside, with the bishop on its best diagonal.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 exf4 3.Nf3 Nc6 4.Bc4 g5.strategy: Holds the gambit pawn with the g-pawn, the standard way to keep the extra material. The price is a loosened kingside and a pawn on g5 that White can attack at once, so Black has to be ready for sharp play against the king.
1.e4 e5 2.f4 exf4 3.Nf3 Nc6 4.Bc4 g5.name: King's Gambit Accepted: Blachly Gambit

1.e4 e5 2.f4 exf4 3.Nf3 Nc6 4.Nc3 g5.strategy: The thematic way to keep the gambit pawn: the g-pawn supports f4 and threatens to kick the f3 knight. Black accepts a loosened kingside and invites a sharp fight, in which White's two developed knights give the attack plenty of fuel.

1.e4 e5 2.f4 exf4 3.Nf3 Nc6 4.Nc3 Be7.strategy: Develops with the threat of a check on h4 that can cost White the right to castle, since the king would have to step aside. White gains strong central control, and Black counts on the white king's discomfort to compensate.
1.e4 e5 2.f4 exf4 3.Nf3 Nc6 4.Nc3 Be7.name: Vienna Gambit, with Max Lange Defence: Cunningham Defence
